title: Hierarchical assembly of a Ti_24 metal-organic polyhedron via kinetic trapping of intermediates

paper_content.abstract: The synthesis of high-nuclearity titanium metal-organic polyhedra (Ti-MOPs) has remained a formidable challenge due to the high oxophilicity and hydrolysis susceptibility of Ti4+ ions. Herein, we report a Ti24 MOP with a truncated octahedron (tro) topology, which represents the highest nuclearity Ti-MOP reported to date. Beyond structural characterization, we introduce a pathway intervention strategy using Ni2+ as a kinetic modulator to trap and structurally characterize two key intermediates—a Ti12 macrocycle and a Ti12 (6-4-6) module. These intermediates outline a hierarchical assembly pathway from simple precursors to Ti24 MOP. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this process is governed by a coordination lability gradient between Ti4+ and Ni2+, providing an effective strategy for directing supramolecular complexity. This Ti-MOP exhibits permanent microporosity, gas separation, and post-assembly modification capability. This work transforms a synthetic challenge into a strategic advantage, offering a blueprint for the rational assembly of complex metal-organic architectures.
paper_content.introduction:
The programmable construction of metal-organic polyhedra (MOPs) represents a central goal in supramolecular chemistry1–7, driven by their potential for creating tailored nanocavities with applications in separation, catalysis, and sensing8–12. A significant barrier to achieving this goal is the inherent difficulty in probing self-assembly mechanisms, which typically involve high-energy intermediates13. While in situ techniques such as nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR)14,15, high-resolution mass spectrometry (HRMS)16, and fluorescence spectrum17 can track coordination processes in real time to some extent, they often lack the structural resolution needed to unambiguously identify intermediate species.

This challenge is particularly acute in titanium chemistry, where the high reactivity and oxophilicity of Ti4+ ions18–20 typically lead to the formation of thermodynamically stable titanium-oxo clusters (TOCs)21–25 or metal-organic frameworks (Ti-MOFs)26–30, rather than discrete Ti-MOPs31–34. Since Raymond’s pioneering report on tetrahedral Ti4 MOP in 199835, although certain progress has been made in this field, there are still fewer than 20 types of Ti-MOPs to date31. These structures still have the following limitations: i) low nuclearities (≤18 Ti atoms)34, ii) simplistic topologies such as tetrahedra and cubes36–38 (Fig. 1a), and iii) low modifiability. The lack of structural complexity and functional versatility in known Ti-MOPs highlights a significant gap in the field. Although our group has contributed to this area with the synthesis of a giant cage-like Ti oxo-cluster and several Ti-MOPs36,39–41, the development of high-nuclearity Ti-MOPs with sophisticated architectures remains a formidable challenge, owing to the difficulty in controlling Ti4+ ion reactivity and hydrolysis.

Herein, we have successfully synthesized and determined the crystal structure of FIR-151—a Ti24 MOP with tro topology. This high-symmetry cage not only represents the highest nuclearity Ti-MOP reported to date, but also demonstrates how the inherent challenges of titanium coordination chemistry can be overcome to achieve architectural complexity. The assembly pathway was elucidated through the structural characterization of two key intermediates: a Ti12 macrocycle (FIR-152) and a Ti12 (6-4-6) module (FIR-153). These structures provide direct evidence for a hierarchical assembly pathway (Fig. 1b), underpinned by a coordination lability gradient between Ti4+ and Ni2+. Furthermore, FIR-151 exhibits permanent porosity, selective gas adsorption, and post-assembly modification capabilities, demonstrating functional relevance. This work not only advances the understanding of titanium supramolecular chemistry but also establishes an effective strategy for achieving programmable synthesis in dynamic metal-organic systems.
paper_content.results:
Squaric acid (H2C4O4) is frequently employed as an organic template to facilitate the ring expansion and assembly of macrocyclic compounds42. In existing titanium complexes, it has been observed that the C4O42– ligand coordinates with four Ti4+ ions to form a 4-membered ring module43,44. Such modules are often found in complex polyhedral structures, exhibiting topological types such as sod, rho, and lta. Here, we select Ti4+ ions and C4O42– ligands for assembly to construct polyhedral featuring intricate topological architectures. The reaction of Ti(OiPr)4 with H2C4O4 in the mixture solvent of acetic acid (CH3COOH)/acetonitrile (CH3CN) at 120°C led to the formation of yellow rhombic dodecahedral crystals of FIR-151 (FIR = Fujian Institute Research; Supplementary Fig. 1). Single-crystal X-ray diffraction (SCXRD) analysis reveals that FIR-151 crystallizes in the tetragonal P4/nmc space group with the formula as Ti24O24(C4O4)6(CH3COO)36 · guest (Supplementary Fig. 2 and Table S1). Its structure features a Ti24 MOP with a tro topology, representing the highest nuclearity Ti-MOP reported to date (Fig. 2a).

To elucidate the structure of FIR-151, we conducted a detailed analysis (Supplementary Fig. 3). Firstly, twelve Ti atoms are bridged by twelve μ2-O atoms to form a Ti12 macrocycle—marking what is, to the best of our knowledge, the first observation of such a Ti12 structure (Supplementary Table S2). This ring is capped by eighteen terminally coordinated CH3COO– ligands. Then, one C4O42– ligand positions within the central pore of the Ti12 ring, coordinating to four Ti atoms, leading to the formation of a Ti12 (6-4-6) module. Four additional C4O42– ligands occupy the remaining coordination sites on the Ti atoms within this module. The incorporation of C4O42– induces a conformational change in the Ti12 macrocycle, causing it to narrow and bend into a distinct roof-like architecture. This contrasts sharply with the planar or S-shaped configurations typically found in other wheel-type TOCs (Supplementary Fig. 4)25. The cage structure of FIR-151 can be viewed as a dimer of two Ti12 (6-4-6) modules via four shared C4O42– ligands (Fig. 2b and Supplementary Fig. 5). The assembly pathway of FIR-151, involving the dimerization of two curved Ti12 (6-4-6) modules, is reminiscent of the formation of iconic supramolecular structures such as the ‘tennis ball’ capsule45. In that system, two identical, curved organic subunits self-assemble through hydrogen bonds to form a closed spheroidal cavity capable of encapsulating guest molecules. The convergence of this geometric design principle across both organic hydrogen-bonded systems and inorganic MOPs underscores its universality for constructing closed-shell nanostructures from pre-organized, curved building blocks. As such, the overall assembly can be topologically represented as a truncated octahedron with the point symbol (46.68) (Fig. 2c). It is noteworthy that the square faces in the topological representation are realized as rectangles in the actual structure; this geometric distortion does not affect the topological classification. To the best of our knowledge, this structure provides an instance of a tro-type topology in Ti-MOP (Supplementary Table S3). The resulting structure measures approximately 18.7 × 18.7 × 20.2 Å3 and features a spherical inner cavity with a diameter of roughly 10.0 Å. Electrostatic potential (ESP) calculations reveal that FIR-151 is electrically neutral overall, yet features negatively charged open windows that favor interaction with cationic guest species (Supplementary Fig. 6). Moreover, these cages adopt a body-centered cubic close-packed arrangement in FIR-151 (Supplementary Fig. 7).

To deconvolute the pathway leading to this MOP, we designed a strategy to perturb the assembly equilibrium using kinetic trappers, aiming to stabilize and isolate metastable intermediates for structural characterization (Supplementary Fig. 8).

Intervention I: Trapping a macrocyclic precursor with Ni2+. Introducing NiCl2·6H2O into the reaction mixture leads to the isolation of yellow block-shaped crystals of FIR-152 (Supplementary Fig. 9). SCXRD analysis reveals that it crystallizes in the monoclinic space group P2/n. Its structure is represented by the formula [Ni(CH3CN)6]2+·[Ti12Ni2O6Cl4(C4O4)8(CH3COO)18(CH3CN)6]2– (Supplementary Table S4), and is built around Ti12 macrocycle—corresponding to intermediate 1 (Fig. 2d). Two NiCl3 clusters are positioned above and below the Ti12 macrocycle and are connected to it via three C4O42– ligands, forming a heterometallic MOP, FIR-152. The incorporation of the two NiCl3 clusters (Fig. 2e) results in a chair-like configuration of the Ti12 macrocycle ring. We propose that Ni2+ acts as a kinetic trap for this oligomeric species by modulating the local coordination thermodynamics, thereby stabilizing a critical nucleation intermediate along the assembly pathway.

Intervention II: Directing evolution with quaternary ammonium ions. When tetrabutylammonium bromide (TBAB) was introduced under otherwise identical reaction conditions, a structural rearrangement occurred, leading to the formation of orange hexagonal dipyramid crystals assigned as the isomeric phase FIR-153 (space group Cmcm, Supplementary Fig. 10 and Table S4). This compound features a Ti12 (6-4-6) modular structure (intermediate 2, Fig. 2f) in which the original 12-membered ring adopts a boat conformation. A central C4O42– ligand partitions the ring via coordination to four Ti4+ ions, while two NiCl3 clusters reposition to apical sites, linked by additional C4O42– ligands to form an isomeric MOP. Here, Ni2+ again serves to kinetically trap this reconfigured module. This transformation demonstrates how non-coordinating additives can profoundly influence the assembly landscape, steering the reorganization of a metastable intermediate into a non-pathway structural motif preceding the final MOP. The molecular structures of both intermediates, FIR-152 and FIR-153, were corroborated in solution by 1H NMR and small-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS) techniques (Supplementary Figs. 11–14).

To elucidate the assembly pathway of FIR-151, we employed a combination of solution-phase, structural, and reactivity analyses. Real-time SAXS monitoring revealed a continuous evolution of the maximum particle dimension (Dmax), as derived from the pair distance distribution function, P(r), from an initial ~6.7 Å through discrete states (~9.5 Å, ~17.0 Å) to the final ~19.1 Å (Supplementary Fig. 15). This progression is consistent with a multi-step assembly process rather than a single-step reaction. To gain atomic-level insight into potential intermediates along this pathway, we introduced Ni2+ ions as a kinetic trap, successfully isolating two key structural modules: the Ti12 macrocycle (FIR-152) and the Ti12 (6-4-6) module (FIR-153). Their precise structural complementarity provides a plausible geometric model for the progression towards the final cage. Critical reactivity tests further support this interpretation: while FIR-151 forms efficiently in the absence of Ni2+, the Ni2+-stabilized FIR-153 cannot be converted to the final product under identical conditions. This indicates that Ni2+ acts to trap and stabilize transient, on-pathway species, which would otherwise be unobservable. While each line of evidence—solution dynamics, structural correlation, and chemical reactivity—has inherent limitations, their convergence mutually supports a coherent, hierarchical assembly pathway from simple precursors to the complex Ti24 architecture.

Comparative analysis of the intermediates and the final product with precise crystal structures allows us to propose a hierarchical assembly pathway: Ti12 macrocycle (intervention 1) → Reorganization → Ti12 (6-4-6) module (intervention 2) → Dimerization → Ti24 MOP (Fig. 3a). This mechanistic proposal is best regarded as a robust working hypothesis, substantiated by the convergence of multiple experimental observations within the current technical constraints. We acknowledge that definitive proof would require direct molecular-level tracking of the transient intermediates in solution. Nevertheless, this hypothesis provides a valuable structural and conceptual framework for understanding the complex self-assembly of high-nuclearity MOPs and paves the way for future investigations using advanced in situ techniques.

This work supplies an effective strategy that extends beyond a single case study: the strategic use of coordination lability gradients (Fig. 3b). The assembly is controlled by the differential kinetics between the highly labile Ti4+ ion, which drives dynamic reorganization, and the moderately labile Ni2+ ion, which acts as a kinetic trap to stabilize key intermediates at defined points along the pathway. This strategy of using a second metal ion to modulate the energy landscape of a primary assembly process offers an alternative approach to achieve structural complexity, and its broad utility awaits validation in other metal-organic systems.

The as-synthesized FIR-151 were further characterized using various analytical techniques to confirm their phase purity, thermal stabilities, optical bandgap, and photoactivity (Supplementary Figs. 16–22). FIR-151 exhibit high stability towards common organic solvents and some acids and bases (Supplementary Fig. 23), enabling investigation of its gas adsorption and separation properties. To evaluate its porosity, the solvent-exchanged sample (CH3CN) was activated under vacuum at 30°C for 12 h (Supplementary Fig. 24). N2 sorption isotherms measured at 77 K revealed a type I isotherm, confirming the microporous nature and permanent porosity of FIR-151 (Fig. 4a). The Brunauer–Emmett–Teller (BET) and Langmuir surface areas were calculated to be 703 and 859 m2·g–1 (Supplementary Fig. 25), respectively—significantly higher than those of most reported MOPs2,46. The total pore volume, estimated from the N2 uptake at a relative pressure of P/P0 = 0.998, is 0.322 cm3·g–1 (Supplementary Fig. 26). Density functional theory (DFT) pore size distribution analysis further indicated a predominant pore width of 7.5 Å (Fig. 4b).

Leveraging its high surface area, we further assessed FIR-151’s gas separation potential via CO2, C2H2, C2H4, and C2H6 sorption at 273 and 298 K (Fig. 4c, d, and Supplementary Figs. 27–31). FIR-151 exhibits a high CO2 uptake capacity of 79 cm3·g–1 at 273 K and 51 cm3·g–1 at 298 K, with an isosteric heat of adsorption (Qst) of 40 kJ·mol–1, indicating strong host-guest interactions within the pores. Furthermore, FIR-151 shows distinct gas uptake profiles for C2 hydrocarbons: under identical conditions, sorption capacities for C2H2, C2H4, and C2H6 were measured as 73, 53, and 35 cm3·g–1 at 273 K, and 60, 38, and 25 cm3·g–1 at 298 K, respectively. The corresponding Qst values are 32, 28, and 27 kJ·mol–1, reflecting differential binding affinities. The notable contrast in both uptake capacity and adsorption enthalpy among these gases underscores the potential of FIR-151 for highly selective gas separation. To quantitatively predict separation selectivity, ideal adsorbed solution theory (IAST) was employed based on the above adsorption results (Supplementary Figs. 32–37). As a result, the predicted selectivity for an equimolar C2H2/C2H6 (v/v = 50:50) mixture reaches 42 at 273 K and 53 at 298 K (Fig. 4e). In addition, FIR-151 also shows favorable selectivities for CO2/C2H6 (v/v = 50:50; 15 at 273 K and 9 at 298 K (Fig. 4f), outperforming most reported MOPs46–48. Furthermore, the structural integrity and permanent porosity of FIR-151 were confirmed by powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD) measurements after gas sorption and the reproducibility of two consecutive BET measurements (Supplementary Fig. 38). These results demonstrate how mechanistic understanding and controlled synthesis of MOPs can yield functional materials49.

Building on the structural insights of FIR-151, we explored its post-assembly modification potential to tailor material properties (Fig. 5a). Specifically, the replacement of acetate ligands in FIR-151 with methacrylate and benzoate to form FIR-154 and FIR-155, respectively. The successful ligand exchange was verified by 1H NMR spectroscopy (Supplementary Figs. 39, 40), while the retention of the intact MOP architecture in solution was confirmed by SAXS (Supplementary Figs. 41 and 42). Furthermore, PXRD spectra confirmed the phase purity of the modified MOPs in the solid state (Supplementary Figs. 43 and 44). SCXRD confirmed that both compounds retain the structural integrity of the parental Ti24 MOP (Supplementary Table S5). Furthermore, all three MOPs adopt a body-centered cubic close-packed arrangement (Fig. 5b–d). The introduction of benzoate groups in FIR-155 enhances the material’s hydrophobicity, as confirmed by contact angle measurements (Supplementary Fig. 45), and facilitates π-π stacking (3.68 Å) between MOPs in its body-centered cubic lattice. Concurrently, the incorporation of methacrylate groups in FIR-154 installs structurally confirmed polymerizable handles, establishing a rational molecular design for exploring chemical functionality tuning and serving as a building block for extended polymeric networks in future studies.
paper_content.methods:
Synthesis of FIR-151
A mixture of Ti(OiPr)4 (0.325 mmol, 100 μL), H2C4O4 (0.1 mmol, 0.011 g), CH3CN (4 mL), and CH3COOH (1 mL) in a 25 mL Teflon-lined stainless-steel autoclave. Then, the mixture was heated at 120°C for 3 days. After cooling to room temperature, the yellow rhombic dodecahedral crystals were washed with a large amount of CH3CN, filtered, and stored in CH3CN (Yield: ∼13.1 mg, ca. 22% based on Ti). One of these crystals was used for X-ray crystallography.

Synthesis of FIR-152
A mixture of Ti(OiPr)4 (0.325 mmol, 100 μL), NiCl2·6H2O (0.2 mmol, 0.048 g), H2C4O4 (0.1 mmol, 0.011 g), CH3CN (4 mL), and CH3COOH (1 mL) in a 20 mL vial. Then, the mixture was heated at 80°C for 7 days. After cooling to room temperature, the yellow block-shaped crystals were washed with CH3CN and stored in CH3CN (Yield: ∼20.0 mg, ca. 33% based on H2C4O4). One of these crystals was used for X-ray crystallography.

Synthesis of FIR-153
A mixture of Ti(OiPr)4 (0.325 mmol, 100 μL), NiCl2·6H2O (0.2 mmol, 0.048 g), H2C4O4 (0.1 mmol, 0.011 g), tetrabutylammonium bromide (TBAB, 0.2 mmol, 0.062 g), CH3CN (4 mL), and CH3COOH (1 mL) in a 20 mL vial. Then, the mixture was heated at 80°C for 7 days. After cooling to room temperature, the orange hexagonal dipyramid crystals were washed with CH3CN and stored in CH3CN (Yield: ∼21.2 mg, ca. 35% based on H2C4O4). One of these crystals was used for X-ray crystallography.

Synthesis of FIR-154
FIR-151 crystals (0.005 g, 1.154 × 10-6 mol) were dissolved in a DMSO/CH3CN mixture (v/v = 1/9, 1 mL) under ultrasonication. Methacrylic acid (0.30 mmol, 25 μL) was then added, and the solution was heated at 80°C for 7 days. After cooling to room temperature, orange crystals of FIR-154 were collected by filtration, washed with CH3CN, and stored in CH3CN (Yield: ∼5.4 mg, ca. 89% based on FIR-151). One of these crystals was used for X-ray crystallography.

Synthesis of FIR-155
FIR-151 crystals (0.005 g, 1.154 × 10-6 mol) were dissolved in a DMSO/CH3CN mixture (v/v = 1/9, 1 mL) under ultrasonication. Benzoic acid (0.30 mmol, 0.036 g) was then added, and the solution was heated at 80°C for 7 days. After cooling to room temperature, yellow single crystals of FIR-155 were collected by filtration, washed with CH3CN, and stored in CH3CN (Yield: ∼6.5 mg, ca. 86% based on FIR-151). One of these crystals was used for X-ray crystallography.

Solvent exchange and activation of FIR-151
Freshly prepared FIR-151 was soaked in CH3CN at room temperature for 7 days to exchange the guest CH3COOH. Subsequently, the samples were activated under dynamic vacuum at 30°C for 12 h. This temperature ensured the complete removal of the solvents, meanwhile excluding the possibility of FIR-151 decomposition.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
This work reports a significant breakthrough in the synthesis of high-nuclearity titanium metal-organic polyhedra (Ti-MOPs).
The authors have not only synthesized a record-high nuclearity Ti-MOP but, more importantly, unveiled a novel 'pathway
intervention' strategy with broad implications for the field of supramolecular assembly. I think this is an excellent and
impactful work that can be published in Nature Communications after minor revision.
1. The authors propose a compelling mechanism where the differential kinetics between Ti4+ and Ni2+ ions control the
assembly pathway. To strengthen the generalizability of this concept, could the authors comment on the selection criteria for
the kinetic trap metal ion? Specifically, what is the rationale for choosing Ni2+ over other moderately labile ions (e.g., Co or
Cu)?
2. The authors state that the sample was activated at 30 °C under vacuum to evaluate porosity. Please provide the
experimental basis for the selection of activation temperature. Comparative gas sorption data should be included to
substantiate that 30 °C is optimal for achieving complete activation and maximum porosity, as opposed to higher
temperatures, which may induce pore collapse or degradation.
3. Please double-check the consistency of compound labels (e.g., FIR-151, FIR-152, FIR-153) and the corresponding
intermediate numbers (Intermediate 1 and Intermediate 2) throughout all figures and the main text for clarity.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
This manuscript reports the synthesis, structural characterization, and further functionalization of a Ti24-based metal-organic
polyhedron (MOP), designated as FIR-151. A notable strength of this work lies in the intriguing structure of Ti24-MOP, which
resembles that of the well-known molecular "tennis ball"—a hydrogen-bonded capsule. The authors also make a valuable
contribution by clearly demonstrating that non-coordinating additives can exert a profound influence on the assembly
structures during synthesis; leveraging these additives, they successfully captured two intermediates and proposed a
logically reasonable assembly mechanism for FIR-151. Furthermore, the experimental data provided comprehensively
characterize the material’s physicochemical properties, and the manuscript is generally well-organized. However, several
issues requiring revision were identified. The manuscript is recommended for publication in Nature Communications after
addressing the following suggestions.
1. Page 4, line 82, the authors describe FIR-151 crystals as “yellow rhombic dodecahedral” and cite Supplementary Fig. 1 in
support. However, this Supplementary Fig. 1 (an SEM image) only exhibits the morphology (rhombic dodecahedral shape)
of the crystals, not their color (yellow). In fact, the photograph in Fig. 5 clearly shows the FIR-151 crystals with the perfect
yellow rhombic dodecahedral appearance, making it the more appropriate reference for the authors’ description.
Additionally, the caption of Supplementary Fig. 1 contains a minor error: the term “images” should be revised to “image” (as
the figure only includes one SEM image).
2. For Figure 2a, the four front-side Ti4+ cations form a rectangle with long edges oriented vertically. In contrast, for Figure
2b, the front-side rectangle formed by 4 Ti-vertices has its long edges oriented horizontally. So the cage structures in the two
figures do not align in the same topological orientation.
3. The caption of Supplementary Fig. 3 should explicitly emphasize that the depicted process represents a proposed
assembly route. While the proposed route is logically reasonable, it should be clarified that this assembly process has not
been directly observed experimentally.
4. The formation mechanism of Ti24-MOP is particularly interesting, as it resembles that of the well-known molecular "tennis
ball"—a hydrogen-bonded capsule (Angew. Chem. Int. Ed., 1993, 32 (12): 1699).
5. Supplementary Fig. 7b appears problematic. It contains numerous vertices that are not connected to the central node,
which makes it difficult to identify the 8-connected mode as described. Additionally, the figure fails to clearly exhibit the cubic
structure corresponding to body-centered cubic (BCC) packing.
6. The authors refer to Ti24-MOP as a truncated octahedral-type MOP. However, according to the structure shown in Fig. 2b,
the front-facing shape is a rectangle rather than a square—a key feature that deviates from the typical truncated octahedron.
Thus, it may be more accurate to term this structure a pseudo-truncated octahedron.
7. Page 8, line 151, the content of this paragraph, when paired with Fig. 3, is somewhat confusing. Specifically, it appears
inconsistent with the actual synthesis process: the synthesis of Ti24-MOF does not require Ni2+ for intermediate stabilization
or trapping, nor does it require TBAB as a template for intermediate configuration.
8. Supplementary Fig. 8, two issues are noted. Firstly, the figure itself does not include the subpanel labels (e.g., (a)/(b)) as
described in its caption. Secondly, the abbreviation “TBTA” in the figure (or caption, as applicable) should be corrected to
“TBAB”.
9. Page 9, line 171, the authors state that FIR-151 exhibits high stability in various organic solvents and cite Supplementary
Fig. 16. However, this figure only shows the cell parameters of the MOP in acetonitrile, not in multiple organic solvents, thus
failing to support the claim of stability across a range of solvents.
10. Page 9, line 179, the description of the method used to obtain the pore volume is somewhat confusing. The authors state
that the pore volume was determined via a single-point method; however, they cite Supplementary Fig. 19—a figure that
presents a pore volume curve with multiple data points (rather than a single-point result) and appears to show cumulative
pore volume, not the single-point pore volume referenced in the text. This creates a clear inconsistency between the stated
measurement method and the supporting figure.
11. The authors measured C2H4 adsorption isotherms for Ti24-MOP (Supplementary Fig. 20) but did not mention them in
the main text. Moreover, these C2H4 isotherms were not plotted together with the isotherms of other gases. This is
inconsistent with Supplementary Fig. 25, which includes all four gas types in the Qst curves.
12. Page 12, line 219, prior to discussing the interactions between MOPs, the authors should first clearly describe the key
reaction outcomes: specifically, the replacement of the original acetate ligands in FIR-151 MOP with methacrylate ligands
(yielding FIR-154) and with benzoate ligands (yielding FIR-155). This foundational information is necessary to
contextualize the subsequent discussion of MOP interactions.
13. The sentence above Fig. 5, the authors propose that the polymerizable groups in FIR-154 hold potential for chemical
functionality tuning, while the aromatic groups in FIR-155 may enable physical property tuning. To further validate these
promising hypotheses, could the authors consider conducting additional simple demonstration experiments based on these
two functionalized Ti24-MOPs? Such experiments would effectively strengthen the support for the proposed tuning potential
and enhance the persuasiveness of this section.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
The paper reports the synthesis of a Ti₄₂ MOP (FIR-151) with a truncated octahedral topology—the largest and most
complex titanium metal-organic polyhedron (Ti-MOP) reported to date. The authors claim to have elucidated its hierarchical
self-assembly pathway through kinetic trapping of two intermediates (FIR-152 and FIR-153) using Ni²⁺ as a modulator. They
further demonstrate porosity, gas separation, and post-assembly modification.
In my opinion, the work is synthetically impressive, but there are several major concerns, specifically conceptual and
experimental points, that I would like the authors to address prior to the acceptance of this manuscript.
Major points to be addressed/discussed:
1. The claim of a hierarchical assembly pathway from Ti₁₂ → Ti₁₂(6-4-6) → Ti₂₄ relies primarily on isolated crystallographic
snapshots. However, there is no direct in situ spectroscopic evidence connecting these hypothetic reaction intermediates to
species that form in solution during a one-pot reaction to obtain the final product. The so-called reaction intermediates,
unless otherwise proven, might represent parallel or side-products that can be synthesized through off-pathway routes,
and not on the main assembly route. The authors must provide solution tracking (e.g. NMR, Mass Spectrometry, SAX, etc.) of the
main reaction path to prove that FIR-152 and 153 are reaction intermediates and not off-track side products. And most
importantly, could the authors confirm if they attempted synthesize FIR-151 under solvothermal conditions in the presence of
FIR-153 and Ni ions?
2. Reported BET area (703 m² g⁻¹) and IAST selectivity values are impressive for a molecular specie, but need a few error
analysis. The activation temperature is set at 30ºC, which is unusually low, and might not ensure complete solvent or
ambient moisture removal. Furthermore, no PXRD data is given after activation, and thus we cannot confirm that the sample
does not suffer a structural rearrangement upon activation. Can the authors show PXRD and BET reproducibility after at
least 2 activation/re-solvation cycles?
3. FIR-151 is said to be “stable in various organic solvents,” but no data on water or acidic/basic stability are shown. Since
Ti4+ ions are prone to hydrolytic susceptibility, the authors need to show the stability of all the species in such media for
properly assessing their potential.
4. In the literature, several Ti-MOPs with varying titanium nuclearities have been reported, and their bulk molecular integrity
and purity are typically verified using spectroscopic techniques such as 1H/13C NMR, DOSY NMR, and mass spectrometry.
Therefore, this manuscript should be supplemented with NMR and MALDI-MS or ESI-MS data for all newly synthesized
titanium structures (FIR-151, FIR-152, FIR-153, FIR-154, and FIR-155) to confirm their bulk composition and phase purity. A
single crystal structure only proves the structure of one crystal, not for the whole bulk sample.
Minor points to be addressed:
1. The yield of all new structures should be provided.
2. In the Supplementary Information, the PXRD pattern shown in Supplementary Figure S33 for the as-synthesized sample
displays significantly fewer and weaker diffraction peaks compared with the simulated pattern. The authors should clarify the
reason for this discrepancy and discuss whether it arises from preferred orientation, partial crystallinity, or sample
degradation.
3. In the Supplementary Information, Supplementary Figure S34 shows that the as-synthesized PXRD pattern exhibits
additional diffraction peaks that are not present in the simulated pattern. The authors should explain the origin of these
discrepancies—as those could indicate the presence of mixed phases or impurities. Additional molecular characterization,
as mentioned in major Point 4, should be conducted to all species to confirm phase purity.
4. As stated in Section 2: Instruments and Characterizations of the Supplementary Information (lines 79–80), several
spectroscopic techniques, including FT-IR, 1H NMR, and 13C NMR, are listed as part of the characterization methods.
However, these corresponding spectra are not provided in the manuscript or Supplementary Information. The authors should
ensure that all characterization methods mentioned are properly documented and supported with the relevant experimental
data and spectra (see Major point 4).
reviewer_comments.reviewer_4:
This study stands as a perfect example of how to combine structural innovation with profound mechanistic elucidation. The
successful synthesis of the Ti24 MOP with truncated octahedron topology is itself a remarkable achievement, given the
significant synthetic challenges of Ti4+ chemistry. By employing Ni2+ ions as kinetic modulators, they have achieved what
many thought impossible: the crystallographic characterization of two key intermediates—a Ti12 macrocycle and a Ti12 (6-
4-6) module. This provides unprecedented, atomic-level insight into the hierarchical assembly pathway. The methodology of
exploiting coordination lability gradients to trap intermediates offers a generalizable blueprint for studying self-assembly
processes across diverse metal-ligand systems. The additional demonstration of permanent porosity and post-assembly
modification further enhances the practical impact of these findings. Therefore, I would like to recommend the manuscript for
publication in Nature Communications, after addressing the following revisions.
Comment 1. Was the 'pathway intervention' strategy attempted with other transition metal ions? If so, please summarize the
outcomes in the supplementary information. Were similar intermediates observed, or did other metals lead to different
products or no modulation at all?
Comment 2. It is crucial to confirm the structural integrity of Ti24 MOP after gas sorption. Please provide the PXRD data of
FIR-151 after gas adsorption in the supplementary information will strongly demonstrate its stability for potential applications.
Comment 3. In Fig. 5b-d, please clearly indicate in the figure captions that the non-covalent interactions between MOPs
(such as hydrogen bonds or π-π interactions) are highlighted with green dotted lines. This clarification is crucial for guiding
readers in interpreting crystal stacking diagrams.
Comment 4. In Supplementary Tables S1 and S3, please provide the complete chemical names for all ligand abbreviations
to ensure clarity and thereby enhance the accessibility and utility of the presented data.

Response to Reviewer #1
This work reports a significant breakthrough in the synthesis of high-nuclearity titanium metal-
organic polyhedra (Ti-MOPs). The authors have not only synthesized a record-high nuclearity
Ti-MOP but, more importantly, unveiled a novel 'pathway intervention' strategy with broad
implications for the field of supramolecular assembly. I think this is an excellent and impactful
work that can be published in Nature Communications after minor revision.
1. The authors propose a compelling mechanism where the differential kinetics between Ti4+
and Ni2+ ions control the assembly pathway. To strengthen the generalizability of this concept,
could the authors comment on the selection criteria for the kinetic trap metal ion? Specifically,
what is the rationale for choosing Ni2+ over other moderately labile ions (e.g., Co or Cu)?
Responses: The reviewer raises a fundamental point regarding our choice of metal ion, which
allows us to elaborate on the design principles behind the kinetic trap. The choice of Ni2+ was
indeed deliberate, based on its unique positioning in what we might call the "coordination
lability landscape".
While several borderline acids like Co2+ or Cu2+ could in principle interact with the
squarate ligand, our working hypothesis was that Ni2+ would provide the optimal kinetic
profile—its ligand exchange rate is slow enough to form metastable complexes that can be
crystallized, yet sufficiently dynamic to allow incorporation during the Ti4+-driven assembly.
This creates the perfect conditions for intervention without a complete pathway shutdown.
The control experiments the reviewer might be wondering about strongly support this
reasoning. When we substituted Cu2+ or Co2+ under otherwise identical conditions, the reaction
proceeded directly to the final Ti MOP without any observable intermediate trapping. These
24
"negative" results are actually quite telling:
With Co2+, we believe its faster ligand exchange kinetics prevent the formation of a stable
enough trap to halt the assembly process. For Cu2+, while it shares the borderline acid
classification, its tendency toward Jahn-Teller distortion leads to preferred geometries that
appear incompatible with the specific coordination environments required in our intermediate
structures.
So in essence, Ni2+ emerged as the unique candidate that provided just the right
combination of moderate lability, geometric flexibility, and binding affinity to make the kinetic
trapping strategy work. This understanding gives us a valuable set of criteria to consider when
extending this approach to other metal-organic systems.
2. The authors state that the sample was activated at 30 °C under vacuum to evaluate porosity.
Please provide the experimental basis for the selection of activation temperature. Comparative
gas sorption data should be included to substantiate that 30 °C is optimal for achieving
complete activation and maximum porosity, as opposed to higher temperatures, which may
induce pore collapse or degradation.
Responses: Thank you for the reviewers' suggestions. The selection of 30 °C as the activation
temperature for FIR-151 is not random. We screened different activation temperatures from 30
to 120 °C and found that as the activation temperature increased, the adsorption uptakes
gradually decreased, possibly due to pore collapse caused by higher temperatures
(Supplementary Figure S24a). Similarly, we also compared the TGA results of as-synthesized,
after CH CN exchange, and activated at 30 °C for FIR-151 (Supplementary Figure S24b). This
3
comparison further confirmed that 30 °C is the optimal activation temperature for this
compound.

and the corresponding intermediate numbers (Intermediate 1 and Intermediate 2) throughout

Responses: Thanks very much for the kind suggestions. We have carefully reviewed and
unified all compound labels and the corresponding intermediate numbers across the text and

Responses: We sincerely thank the reviewer for this exceptionally insightful comment. We

In response, we have incorporated this analogy into the discussion section of our revised

whereas our Ti MOP relies on robust coordination bonds, the underlying geometric

Responses: We thank the reviewer for pointing out the potential ambiguity in Supplementary

these discrete cages lack direct inter-cage connections, we analyzed their spatial arrangement
by treating each cage as a spherical node. Our analysis shows that each node is equidistant from
its eight immediate neighbors. Therefore, when each node is treated as having eight
connections, the entire lattice exhibits a body-centered cubic (bcu) topology. This confirms a
bcu close-packing mode, as opposed to the simple cubic (pcu) packing that was mistakenly
indicated by the initial visualization.
The original figure did not effectively convey this specific topological perspective. We
have therefore replaced it with an improved version that explicitly highlights the central cage
and its eight topological neighbors, which now unambiguously illustrates the bcu packing

Response to Reviewer #3
The paper reports the synthesis of a Ti MOP (FIR-151) with a truncated octahedral
24
topology—the largest and most complex titanium metal-organic polyhedron (Ti-MOP)
reported to date. The authors claim to have elucidated its hierarchical self-assembly pathway
through kinetic trapping of two intermediates (FIR-152 and FIR-153) using Ni2+ as a modulator.
They further demonstrate porosity, gas separation, and post-assembly modification.
In my opinion, the work is synthetically impressive, but there are several major concerns,
specifically conceptual and experimental points, that I would like the authors to address prior
to the acceptance of this manuscript.
Major points to be addressed/discussed:
1. The claim of a hierarchical assembly pathway from Ti → Ti (6-4-6) → Ti relies
12 12 24
primarily on isolated crystallographic snapshots. However, there is no direct in situ
spectroscopic evidence connecting these hypothetic reaction intermediates to species that form
in solution during a one-pot reaction to obtain the final product. The so-called reaction
intermediates, unless otherwise proven, might represent parallel or side-products that can be
synthesized through off-pathway routes, and not on the main assembly route. The authors must
provide solution tracking (e.g. NMR, Mass Spectrometry, SAXS, etc.) of the main reaction
path to prove that FIR-152 and 153 are reaction intermediates and not off-track side products.
And most importantly, could the authors confirm if they attempted synthesize FIR-151 under
solvothermal conditions in the presence of FIR-153 and Ni ions?
Responses: We sincerely thank the reviewer for the insightful comments and rigorous
standards, which have prompted us to reassess our mechanistic interpretation with greater
caution and precision. We fully understand your concern regarding the completeness of the
mechanistic evidence chain, and we would like to clarify, within the scope of our current
experiments, the evidential value and reasonable limits of our mechanistic hypothesis. We
acknowledge that directly observing transient species in Ti4+ systems remains inherently
challenging. To address this, we employed multiple complementary experimental approaches.
First, solution-phase SAXS monitoring (Supplementary Fig. S15) revealed a continuous
evolution in particle size (D ) from ~6.7 Å through discrete intermediates (~9.5 Å and ~17.0
max
Å) to a final value of ~19.1 Å, suggesting a stepwise rather than a single-step assembly process
(Chem. Soc. Rev. 2011, 40, 1006). Second, using a Ni2+ stabilization strategy, we successfully
isolated two structurally complementary modules, the Ti macrocycle and Ti (6-4-6) unit,
12 12
whose geometrical matching provides a reasonable structural rationale for the formation of the
final Ti cage. Third, reactivity tests demonstrated that FIR-151 can be efficiently obtained
24
under Ni2+-free solvothermal conditions, whereas the Ni2+-stabilized FIR-153 cannot be
converted under identical conditions, highlighting the critical kinetic trapping effect of Ni2+ in
capturing transient intermediates (Chem. Soc. Rev. 2017, 46, 3431).
Together, these three sets of independent observations—from dynamic evolution,
structural correlation, and reactivity behavior—mutually support a coherent picture of a
multistep assembly process (Chem. Rev. 2014, 114, 9645). We fully recognize that each line of
evidence has its limitations: SAXS data lack molecular specificity; the proposed ‘structural
complementarity’ is primarily geometrical rather than quantitatively proven; and the reactivity
tests could, in principle, admit multiple interpretations. Nevertheless, the convergence of these
observations points to a structurally correlated and kinetically interpretable multistep assembly
pathway, in which the system likely proceeds through several stabilized intermediate states
toward the final structure.
We are transparent in acknowledging that the current data do not constitute definitive
proof of the mechanism but rather represent a technically constrained, yet informative,
exploration of a complex self-assembly process. The proposed hierarchical pathway should
therefore be regarded as a reasonable and testable working hypothesis, valuable for providing
a structural framework and experimental basis for subsequent investigations. We fully agree
with the reviewer that direct molecular-level evidence—such as in situ spectroscopic tracking
or theoretical modeling—will be essential to further verify and refine this mechanism.
Despite these limitations, we believe that the present study offers meaningful structural
insights and experimental references for understanding the intricate self-assembly behavior of
titanium-oxo systems. We will explicitly clarify the inferential nature and scope of our
mechanistic discussion in the revised manuscript and look forward to advancing this
hierarchical assembly model through more advanced techniques in future work.
Supplementary Figure S15. Ex-situ SAXS monitoring of FIR-151 assembly. (a)
Experimental SAXS diffraction signal and (b) interatomic distance distribution function P(r) at
various reaction times.

specie, but need a few error analysis. The activation temperature is set at 30ºC, which is
unusually low, and might not ensure complete solvent or ambient moisture removal.
Furthermore, no PXRD data is given after activation, and thus we cannot confirm that the
sample does not suffer a structural rearrangement upon activation. Can the authors show PXRD
and BET reproducibility after at least 2 activation/re-solvation cycles?

experiments to fully address these concerns, as summarized below and supported by new data
in the Supplementary Figs. S24 and S38.
1. Optimization of activation temperature: The selection of 30 °C as the activation temperature
was the result of a systematic screening process. As shown in the Reviewer-Only Figure 2a,
N -sorption isotherms were measured for samples activated at temperatures ranging from 30 °C

damage at elevated temperatures. This confirms that 30 °C is indeed the optimal and sufficient

corroborated by TGA data (Reviewer-Only Figure 2b). The analysis confirms the complete
removal of solvent molecules after activation at this temperature.

4. In the literature, several Ti-MOPs with varying titanium nuclearities have been reported, and
their bulk molecular integrity and purity are typically verified using spectroscopic techniques
such as 1H/13C NMR, DOSY NMR, and mass spectrometry. Therefore, this manuscript should
be supplemented with NMR and MALDI-MS or ESI-MS data for all newly synthesized
titanium structures (FIR-151, FIR-152, FIR-153, FIR-154, and FIR-155) to confirm their bulk
composition and phase purity. A single crystal structure only proves the structure of one crystal,
not for the whole bulk sample.
Responses: We would like to express our gratitude to the reviewers for their critical comments
regarding the necessity of verifying the bulk purity and molecular integrity of our newly
synthesized Ti-MOPs. We fully agree that comprehensive characterization beyond SCXRD is
crucial. To directly address this point, we conducted a comprehensive and systematic
characterization study. Convergent evidence from multiple complementary techniques now
supports the bulk composition, phase purity, and structural integrity of all compounds (FIR-
151 to FIR-155). Our comprehensive research methods and main findings are summarized as
follows.
1. NMR spectroscopy:
(1) 1H NMR: We successfully obtained high-quality 1H NMR spectra for all five compounds.
All spectra exhibited sharp and well-resolved signals, with chemical shifts and integral ratios
consistent with the expected cage structure, providing fundamental evidence for their bulk
chemical composition and purity in solution.
(2) Other one-dimensional/two-dimensional NMR: In response to the reviewer's specific
mention of cage structural integrity, we conducted 13C NMR and DOSY experiments.
In 13C NMR, due to the low mass fraction of the squaric acid ligand and the limited
solubility of these samples, even after long-term acquisition (>12 hours), the characteristic
signal of the squaric acid ligand was not observed. However, the signals of all other organic
ligands (acetic acid, methacrylic acid, benzoic acid, acetonitrile) were clearly identifiable and
could be identified.
Crucially, we performed DOSY NMR on the representative compound FIR-155, and the
spectrum showed consistent diffusion coefficients, confirming the presence of monodisperse
cage structures in solution and ruling out the possibility of other impurities.
2. Mass spectrometry analysis:
We fully recognize the value of mass spectrometry data. We extensively attempted both
ESI-MS and MALDI-TOF MS under various conditions, including changes in solvents,
concentrations, ionization parameters, and matrices. Despite these systematic efforts, we were
unable to detect any complete molecular ions of the MOPs. Instead, we consistently observed
only fragment signals with low mass-to-charge ratios—a result that recurred across all
compounds and techniques. This strongly indicates a fundamental challenge: the inherent
instability of such high-nuclearity MOPs under the vacuum and ionization conditions required
for mass spectrometry. Our claim of "extensive effort" is supported by a rigorous (though
ultimately unsuccessful) experimental process. Spectra from these attempts are available upon
request.
3. Small-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS):
To directly and clearly probe the size and integrity of the MOPs in solution, we performed
SAXS measurements.

(1) Impurity signals in the original ¹H NMR spectra
We agree that the earlier spectra displayed weak resonances assignable to residual carboxylic
acids and acetate. These species originate from surface-adsorbed or lattice-included guests
associated with the ligand-exchange synthesis, rather than from the MOP framework itself.
This interpretation aligns with the single-crystal XRD data, which shows complete ligand
exchange at the cage surface.
To isolate the framework signals exclusively, the original batches were subjected to a strict
multi-cycle washing protocol using anhydrous CH₃CN, a non-coordinating solvent that
removes guest molecules without perturbing the coordination structure.
The updated ¹H NMR spectra (Supplementary Figs. 39–40) show complete disappearance of
all previously noted impurity peaks while all framework resonances remain unchanged. No
new signals appear after purification. This confirms that the earlier features originated from
removable guest species rather than structural defects, as the framework signatures are
unaffected by the washing process.
(2) Signals 4 and 5 and solution-phase behavior
The reviewer’s observation regarding signals 4 and 5 is well taken. Our re-analysis indicates
that their appearance in the initial spectra was caused by the use of pure DMSO-d₆, a strongly
coordinating solvent capable of inducing minor, reversible perturbations in metal–carboxylate
environments. Such perturbations do not involve irreversible ligand dissociation.
To assess the species present under conditions relevant to our study, we re-recorded the spectra
in CD₃CN containing only minimal DMSO-d₆ for solubility—the solvent environment
employed in our synthesis, crystallization, and SAXS experiments.
In this representative solvent system, signals 4 and 5 are absent. Only the resonances expected
for the intact cages are observed, and no signals corresponding to free ligand or decomposition
products are detected.
These observations show that:
 The features observed in pure DMSO arise from solvent-induced coordination
perturbations rather than structural dissociation.
 Under all chemically relevant conditions used in this work, the MOPs display
spectroscopic signatures fully consistent with intact cages.
 No evidence for ligand liberation or framework decomposition was detected under any
of the conditions relevant to our workflow.
Therefore, the new results support the conclusions that:
 FIR-154 and FIR-155 are structurally pure; the initial impurity peaks were due to
removable guest species.
 The cages exhibit stable, intact spectroscopic signatures in the CD₃CN/DMSO-d₆
environment central to synthesis and characterization.
 The earlier concerning signals were artifacts specific to pure DMSO and not
representative of the materials’ behavior under the experimental conditions used in this
study.

appreciate the reviewer’s comments, which led to a clearer and more rigorous characterization.

You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

The synthesis of high-nuclearity titanium metal-organic polyhedra (Ti-MOPs) has remained a formidable challenge due to the high oxophilicity and hydrolysis susceptibility of Ti4+ ions. Herein, we report a Ti24 MOP with a truncated octahedron (tro) topology, which represents the highest nuclearity Ti-MOP reported to date. Beyond structural characterization, we introduce a pathway intervention strategy using Ni2+ as a kinetic modulator to trap and structurally characterize two key intermediates—a Ti12 macrocycle and a Ti12 (6-4-6) module. These intermediates outline a hierarchical assembly pathway from simple precursors to Ti24 MOP. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this process is governed by a coordination lability gradient between Ti4+ and Ni2+, providing an effective strategy for directing supramolecular complexity. This Ti-MOP exhibits permanent microporosity, gas separation, and post-assembly modification capability. This work transforms a synthetic challenge into a strategic advantage, offering a blueprint for the rational assembly of complex metal-organic architectures.

---

## Introduction

The programmable construction of metal-organic polyhedra (MOPs) represents a central goal in supramolecular chemistry1–7, driven by their potential for creating tailored nanocavities with applications in separation, catalysis, and sensing8–12. A significant barrier to achieving this goal is the inherent difficulty in probing self-assembly mechanisms, which typically involve high-energy intermediates13. While in situ techniques such as nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR)14,15, high-resolution mass spectrometry (HRMS)16, and fluorescence spectrum17 can track coordination processes in real time to some extent, they often lack the structural resolution needed to unambiguously identify intermediate species.

This challenge is particularly acute in titanium chemistry, where the high reactivity and oxophilicity of Ti4+ ions18–20 typically lead to the formation of thermodynamically stable titanium-oxo clusters (TOCs)21–25 or metal-organic frameworks (Ti-MOFs)26–30, rather than discrete Ti-MOPs31–34. Since Raymond’s pioneering report on tetrahedral Ti4 MOP in 199835, although certain progress has been made in this field, there are still fewer than 20 types of Ti-MOPs to date31. These structures still have the following limitations: i) low nuclearities (≤18 Ti atoms)34, ii) simplistic topologies such as tetrahedra and cubes36–38 (Fig. 1a), and iii) low modifiability. The lack of structural complexity and functional versatility in known Ti-MOPs highlights a significant gap in the field. Although our group has contributed to this area with the synthesis of a giant cage-like Ti oxo-cluster and several Ti-MOPs36,39–41, the development of high-nuclearity Ti-MOPs with sophisticated architectures remains a formidable challenge, owing to the difficulty in controlling Ti4+ ion reactivity and hydrolysis.

Herein, we have successfully synthesized and determined the crystal structure of FIR-151—a Ti24 MOP with tro topology. This high-symmetry cage not only represents the highest nuclearity Ti-MOP reported to date, but also demonstrates how the inherent challenges of titanium coordination chemistry can be overcome to achieve architectural complexity. The assembly pathway was elucidated through the structural characterization of two key intermediates: a Ti12 macrocycle (FIR-152) and a Ti12 (6-4-6) module (FIR-153). These structures provide direct evidence for a hierarchical assembly pathway (Fig. 1b), underpinned by a coordination lability gradient between Ti4+ and Ni2+. Furthermore, FIR-151 exhibits permanent porosity, selective gas adsorption, and post-assembly modification capabilities, demonstrating functional relevance. This work not only advances the understanding of titanium supramolecular chemistry but also establishes an effective strategy for achieving programmable synthesis in dynamic metal-organic systems.

---

## Results

Squaric acid (H2C4O4) is frequently employed as an organic template to facilitate the ring expansion and assembly of macrocyclic compounds42. In existing titanium complexes, it has been observed that the C4O42– ligand coordinates with four Ti4+ ions to form a 4-membered ring module43,44. Such modules are often found in complex polyhedral structures, exhibiting topological types such as sod, rho, and lta. Here, we select Ti4+ ions and C4O42– ligands for assembly to construct polyhedral featuring intricate topological architectures. The reaction of Ti(OiPr)4 with H2C4O4 in the mixture solvent of acetic acid (CH3COOH)/acetonitrile (CH3CN) at 120°C led to the formation of yellow rhombic dodecahedral crystals of FIR-151 (FIR = Fujian Institute Research; Supplementary Fig. 1). Single-crystal X-ray diffraction (SCXRD) analysis reveals that FIR-151 crystallizes in the tetragonal P4/nmc space group with the formula as Ti24O24(C4O4)6(CH3COO)36 · guest (Supplementary Fig. 2 and Table S1). Its structure features a Ti24 MOP with a tro topology, representing the highest nuclearity Ti-MOP reported to date (Fig. 2a).

To elucidate the structure of FIR-151, we conducted a detailed analysis (Supplementary Fig. 3). Firstly, twelve Ti atoms are bridged by twelve μ2-O atoms to form a Ti12 macrocycle—marking what is, to the best of our knowledge, the first observation of such a Ti12 structure (Supplementary Table S2). This ring is capped by eighteen terminally coordinated CH3COO– ligands. Then, one C4O42– ligand positions within the central pore of the Ti12 ring, coordinating to four Ti atoms, leading to the formation of a Ti12 (6-4-6) module. Four additional C4O42– ligands occupy the remaining coordination sites on the Ti atoms within this module. The incorporation of C4O42– induces a conformational change in the Ti12 macrocycle, causing it to narrow and bend into a distinct roof-like architecture. This contrasts sharply with the planar or S-shaped configurations typically found in other wheel-type TOCs (Supplementary Fig. 4)25. The cage structure of FIR-151 can be viewed as a dimer of two Ti12 (6-4-6) modules via four shared C4O42– ligands (Fig. 2b and Supplementary Fig. 5). The assembly pathway of FIR-151, involving the dimerization of two curved Ti12 (6-4-6) modules, is reminiscent of the formation of iconic supramolecular structures such as the ‘tennis ball’ capsule45. In that system, two identical, curved organic subunits self-assemble through hydrogen bonds to form a closed spheroidal cavity capable of encapsulating guest molecules. The convergence of this geometric design principle across both organic hydrogen-bonded systems and inorganic MOPs underscores its universality for constructing closed-shell nanostructures from pre-organized, curved building blocks. As such, the overall assembly can be topologically represented as a truncated octahedron with the point symbol (46.68) (Fig. 2c). It is noteworthy that the square faces in the topological representation are realized as rectangles in the actual structure; this geometric distortion does not affect the topological classification. To the best of our knowledge, this structure provides an instance of a tro-type topology in Ti-MOP (Supplementary Table S3). The resulting structure measures approximately 18.7 × 18.7 × 20.2 Å3 and features a spherical inner cavity with a diameter of roughly 10.0 Å. Electrostatic potential (ESP) calculations reveal that FIR-151 is electrically neutral overall, yet features negatively charged open windows that favor interaction with cationic guest species (Supplementary Fig. 6). Moreover, these cages adopt a body-centered cubic close-packed arrangement in FIR-151 (Supplementary Fig. 7).

To deconvolute the pathway leading to this MOP, we designed a strategy to perturb the assembly equilibrium using kinetic trappers, aiming to stabilize and isolate metastable intermediates for structural characterization (Supplementary Fig. 8).

Intervention I: Trapping a macrocyclic precursor with Ni2+. Introducing NiCl2·6H2O into the reaction mixture leads to the isolation of yellow block-shaped crystals of FIR-152 (Supplementary Fig. 9). SCXRD analysis reveals that it crystallizes in the monoclinic space group P2/n. Its structure is represented by the formula [Ni(CH3CN)6]2+·[Ti12Ni2O6Cl4(C4O4)8(CH3COO)18(CH3CN)6]2– (Supplementary Table S4), and is built around Ti12 macrocycle—corresponding to intermediate 1 (Fig. 2d). Two NiCl3 clusters are positioned above and below the Ti12 macrocycle and are connected to it via three C4O42– ligands, forming a heterometallic MOP, FIR-152. The incorporation of the two NiCl3 clusters (Fig. 2e) results in a chair-like configuration of the Ti12 macrocycle ring. We propose that Ni2+ acts as a kinetic trap for this oligomeric species by modulating the local coordination thermodynamics, thereby stabilizing a critical nucleation intermediate along the assembly pathway.

Intervention II: Directing evolution with quaternary ammonium ions. When tetrabutylammonium bromide (TBAB) was introduced under otherwise identical reaction conditions, a structural rearrangement occurred, leading to the formation of orange hexagonal dipyramid crystals assigned as the isomeric phase FIR-153 (space group Cmcm, Supplementary Fig. 10 and Table S4). This compound features a Ti12 (6-4-6) modular structure (intermediate 2, Fig. 2f) in which the original 12-membered ring adopts a boat conformation. A central C4O42– ligand partitions the ring via coordination to four Ti4+ ions, while two NiCl3 clusters reposition to apical sites, linked by additional C4O42– ligands to form an isomeric MOP. Here, Ni2+ again serves to kinetically trap this reconfigured module. This transformation demonstrates how non-coordinating additives can profoundly influence the assembly landscape, steering the reorganization of a metastable intermediate into a non-pathway structural motif preceding the final MOP. The molecular structures of both intermediates, FIR-152 and FIR-153, were corroborated in solution by 1H NMR and small-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS) techniques (Supplementary Figs. 11–14).

To elucidate the assembly pathway of FIR-151, we employed a combination of solution-phase, structural, and reactivity analyses. Real-time SAXS monitoring revealed a continuous evolution of the maximum particle dimension (Dmax), as derived from the pair distance distribution function, P(r), from an initial ~6.7 Å through discrete states (~9.5 Å, ~17.0 Å) to the final ~19.1 Å (Supplementary Fig. 15). This progression is consistent with a multi-step assembly process rather than a single-step reaction. To gain atomic-level insight into potential intermediates along this pathway, we introduced Ni2+ ions as a kinetic trap, successfully isolating two key structural modules: the Ti12 macrocycle (FIR-152) and the Ti12 (6-4-6) module (FIR-153). Their precise structural complementarity provides a plausible geometric model for the progression towards the final cage. Critical reactivity tests further support this interpretation: while FIR-151 forms efficiently in the absence of Ni2+, the Ni2+-stabilized FIR-153 cannot be converted to the final product under identical conditions. This indicates that Ni2+ acts to trap and stabilize transient, on-pathway species, which would otherwise be unobservable. While each line of evidence—solution dynamics, structural correlation, and chemical reactivity—has inherent limitations, their convergence mutually supports a coherent, hierarchical assembly pathway from simple precursors to the complex Ti24 architecture.

Comparative analysis of the intermediates and the final product with precise crystal structures allows us to propose a hierarchical assembly pathway: Ti12 macrocycle (intervention 1) → Reorganization → Ti12 (6-4-6) module (intervention 2) → Dimerization → Ti24 MOP (Fig. 3a). This mechanistic proposal is best regarded as a robust working hypothesis, substantiated by the convergence of multiple experimental observations within the current technical constraints. We acknowledge that definitive proof would require direct molecular-level tracking of the transient intermediates in solution. Nevertheless, this hypothesis provides a valuable structural and conceptual framework for understanding the complex self-assembly of high-nuclearity MOPs and paves the way for future investigations using advanced in situ techniques.

This work supplies an effective strategy that extends beyond a single case study: the strategic use of coordination lability gradients (Fig. 3b). The assembly is controlled by the differential kinetics between the highly labile Ti4+ ion, which drives dynamic reorganization, and the moderately labile Ni2+ ion, which acts as a kinetic trap to stabilize key intermediates at defined points along the pathway. This strategy of using a second metal ion to modulate the energy landscape of a primary assembly process offers an alternative approach to achieve structural complexity, and its broad utility awaits validation in other metal-organic systems.

The as-synthesized FIR-151 were further characterized using various analytical techniques to confirm their phase purity, thermal stabilities, optical bandgap, and photoactivity (Supplementary Figs. 16–22). FIR-151 exhibit high stability towards common organic solvents and some acids and bases (Supplementary Fig. 23), enabling investigation of its gas adsorption and separation properties. To evaluate its porosity, the solvent-exchanged sample (CH3CN) was activated under vacuum at 30°C for 12 h (Supplementary Fig. 24). N2 sorption isotherms measured at 77 K revealed a type I isotherm, confirming the microporous nature and permanent porosity of FIR-151 (Fig. 4a). The Brunauer–Emmett–Teller (BET) and Langmuir surface areas were calculated to be 703 and 859 m2·g–1 (Supplementary Fig. 25), respectively—significantly higher than those of most reported MOPs2,46. The total pore volume, estimated from the N2 uptake at a relative pressure of P/P0 = 0.998, is 0.322 cm3·g–1 (Supplementary Fig. 26). Density functional theory (DFT) pore size distribution analysis further indicated a predominant pore width of 7.5 Å (Fig. 4b).

Leveraging its high surface area, we further assessed FIR-151’s gas separation potential via CO2, C2H2, C2H4, and C2H6 sorption at 273 and 298 K (Fig. 4c, d, and Supplementary Figs. 27–31). FIR-151 exhibits a high CO2 uptake capacity of 79 cm3·g–1 at 273 K and 51 cm3·g–1 at 298 K, with an isosteric heat of adsorption (Qst) of 40 kJ·mol–1, indicating strong host-guest interactions within the pores. Furthermore, FIR-151 shows distinct gas uptake profiles for C2 hydrocarbons: under identical conditions, sorption capacities for C2H2, C2H4, and C2H6 were measured as 73, 53, and 35 cm3·g–1 at 273 K, and 60, 38, and 25 cm3·g–1 at 298 K, respectively. The corresponding Qst values are 32, 28, and 27 kJ·mol–1, reflecting differential binding affinities. The notable contrast in both uptake capacity and adsorption enthalpy among these gases underscores the potential of FIR-151 for highly selective gas separation. To quantitatively predict separation selectivity, ideal adsorbed solution theory (IAST) was employed based on the above adsorption results (Supplementary Figs. 32–37). As a result, the predicted selectivity for an equimolar C2H2/C2H6 (v/v = 50:50) mixture reaches 42 at 273 K and 53 at 298 K (Fig. 4e). In addition, FIR-151 also shows favorable selectivities for CO2/C2H6 (v/v = 50:50; 15 at 273 K and 9 at 298 K (Fig. 4f), outperforming most reported MOPs46–48. Furthermore, the structural integrity and permanent porosity of FIR-151 were confirmed by powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD) measurements after gas sorption and the reproducibility of two consecutive BET measurements (Supplementary Fig. 38). These results demonstrate how mechanistic understanding and controlled synthesis of MOPs can yield functional materials49.

Building on the structural insights of FIR-151, we explored its post-assembly modification potential to tailor material properties (Fig. 5a). Specifically, the replacement of acetate ligands in FIR-151 with methacrylate and benzoate to form FIR-154 and FIR-155, respectively. The successful ligand exchange was verified by 1H NMR spectroscopy (Supplementary Figs. 39, 40), while the retention of the intact MOP architecture in solution was confirmed by SAXS (Supplementary Figs. 41 and 42). Furthermore, PXRD spectra confirmed the phase purity of the modified MOPs in the solid state (Supplementary Figs. 43 and 44). SCXRD confirmed that both compounds retain the structural integrity of the parental Ti24 MOP (Supplementary Table S5). Furthermore, all three MOPs adopt a body-centered cubic close-packed arrangement (Fig. 5b–d). The introduction of benzoate groups in FIR-155 enhances the material’s hydrophobicity, as confirmed by contact angle measurements (Supplementary Fig. 45), and facilitates π-π stacking (3.68 Å) between MOPs in its body-centered cubic lattice. Concurrently, the incorporation of methacrylate groups in FIR-154 installs structurally confirmed polymerizable handles, establishing a rational molecular design for exploring chemical functionality tuning and serving as a building block for extended polymeric networks in future studies.

---

## Methods

Synthesis of FIR-151
A mixture of Ti(OiPr)4 (0.325 mmol, 100 μL), H2C4O4 (0.1 mmol, 0.011 g), CH3CN (4 mL), and CH3COOH (1 mL) in a 25 mL Teflon-lined stainless-steel autoclave. Then, the mixture was heated at 120°C for 3 days. After cooling to room temperature, the yellow rhombic dodecahedral crystals were washed with a large amount of CH3CN, filtered, and stored in CH3CN (Yield: ∼13.1 mg, ca. 22% based on Ti). One of these crystals was used for X-ray crystallography.

Synthesis of FIR-152
A mixture of Ti(OiPr)4 (0.325 mmol, 100 μL), NiCl2·6H2O (0.2 mmol, 0.048 g), H2C4O4 (0.1 mmol, 0.011 g), CH3CN (4 mL), and CH3COOH (1 mL) in a 20 mL vial. Then, the mixture was heated at 80°C for 7 days. After cooling to room temperature, the yellow block-shaped crystals were washed with CH3CN and stored in CH3CN (Yield: ∼20.0 mg, ca. 33% based on H2C4O4). One of these crystals was used for X-ray crystallography.

Synthesis of FIR-153
A mixture of Ti(OiPr)4 (0.325 mmol, 100 μL), NiCl2·6H2O (0.2 mmol, 0.048 g), H2C4O4 (0.1 mmol, 0.011 g), tetrabutylammonium bromide (TBAB, 0.2 mmol, 0.062 g), CH3CN (4 mL), and CH3COOH (1 mL) in a 20 mL vial. Then, the mixture was heated at 80°C for 7 days. After cooling to room temperature, the orange hexagonal dipyramid crystals were washed with CH3CN and stored in CH3CN (Yield: ∼21.2 mg, ca. 35% based on H2C4O4). One of these crystals was used for X-ray crystallography.

Synthesis of FIR-154
FIR-151 crystals (0.005 g, 1.154 × 10-6 mol) were dissolved in a DMSO/CH3CN mixture (v/v = 1/9, 1 mL) under ultrasonication. Methacrylic acid (0.30 mmol, 25 μL) was then added, and the solution was heated at 80°C for 7 days. After cooling to room temperature, orange crystals of FIR-154 were collected by filtration, washed with CH3CN, and stored in CH3CN (Yield: ∼5.4 mg, ca. 89% based on FIR-151). One of these crystals was used for X-ray crystallography.

Synthesis of FIR-155
FIR-151 crystals (0.005 g, 1.154 × 10-6 mol) were dissolved in a DMSO/CH3CN mixture (v/v = 1/9, 1 mL) under ultrasonication. Benzoic acid (0.30 mmol, 0.036 g) was then added, and the solution was heated at 80°C for 7 days. After cooling to room temperature, yellow single crystals of FIR-155 were collected by filtration, washed with CH3CN, and stored in CH3CN (Yield: ∼6.5 mg, ca. 86% based on FIR-151). One of these crystals was used for X-ray crystallography.

Solvent exchange and activation of FIR-151
Freshly prepared FIR-151 was soaked in CH3CN at room temperature for 7 days to exchange the guest CH3COOH. Subsequently, the samples were activated under dynamic vacuum at 30°C for 12 h. This temperature ensured the complete removal of the solvents, meanwhile excluding the possibility of FIR-151 decomposition.
